title: Centaurus A captured by the Dark Energy Camera
caption: The galaxy Centaurus A, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA Acknowledgments: PI: M. Soraisam (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign/NSF NOIRLab) Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A luminous glow of stars surrounds dark tendrils of dust that hide the bright centre of Centaurus A. Red clouds of hydrogen and, at each end of that dark lane, large numbers of faint blue stars show where new stars are being born.

Seen toward the southern constellation Centaurus, the Centaur, Centaurus A lies more than 12 million light-years away. Its dust is left over from a collision in the past, when a giant elliptical galaxy absorbed a smaller spiral.

The merger did more than add dust. Along with large amounts of gas, the dust lane now hosts star formation across wide areas, and the red hydrogen clouds and many faint blue stars are the evidence. Collisions like this are a reminder that galaxies grow and change by swallowing one another, and that such events can spark fresh generations of stars.
scale: Centaurus A lies more than 12 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: DECam on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed Centaurus A through u, g, r, i and z filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter, covering near-ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light; the colours assigned to each filter are not published.

understand.eye: The z filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the camera's long exposures bring out faint blue stars that would be invisible by eye.
